name: Ottomanism
summary: Ottomanism, the Tanzimat-era state ideology (1839-1876), sought to bind the empire's Muslim and non-Muslim communities into one civic Ottoman nationality with equal rights and duties under the Sultan's dynasty. It paired legal equality, merit-based office, secured property and a constitution with an indivisible state, an Islamic state religion and the retention of communal religious privileges.
scope: The civic Ottomanism of the Tanzimat and the 1876 constitutional programme (Rescripts of 1839 and 1856, the 1876 Constitution, Midhat Pasha and the Young Ottomans), as a state doctrine. It excludes Hamidian pan-Islamism, Pan-Turkism and later Turkish nationalism, and only partly the Young Ottomans' distinct Islamic constitutionalism (noted as a split).

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: The Constitution guarantees the dynasty its property and civil list (Art. 6) and keeps hereditary sovereignty (Art. 3), and the Rescript confirms communal privileges.

bound-labor.rationale: Art. 24 prohibits forced labour (corvee) and confiscation of property, outside wartime exigencies.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Arts. 80 and 96-102 require the Chamber of Deputies to examine and vote the budget and make all taxes depend on law.

clerical-rule.rationale: Sovereign authority rests with the Sultan, who appoints the Seyhulislam (Art. 27), not with senior religious scholars.

conscription.rationale: The Rescript extends the Law of Recruitment to non-Muslims and orders a complete law on their army service.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Elected deputies (Art. 66) and Kemal's popular sovereignty point one way, hereditary sovereignty (Art. 3) the other.

decide-locally.rationale: Art. 108 bases provincial administration on decentralization and Art. 112 provides elected municipal councils, within an indivisible empire.

elective-rulers.rationale: Art. 3 gives sovereignty to the eldest prince of the House of Osman by long-established rule, not by election.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Art. 113 lets the government proclaim a state of siege that temporarily suspends the civil laws, and Art. 36 allows emergency measures with the force of law.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Art. 115 bars suspending any provision and Art. 116 requires two-thirds of both chambers plus the Sultan to amend it.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Art. 17 of the 1876 Constitution makes all Ottomans equal in law with the same rights and duties regardless of religion, and the 1856 Rescript removes distinctions of religion, language or race; the guarantee covers subjects, not explicitly women.

ethnic-nation.rationale: The Rescript abolishes every designation making a class inferior by religion, language or race, and Ottomanism is a civic identity devoid of ethnic underpinnings.

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: The Rescript states it shall be lawful for foreigners to possess landed property under the common laws and charges.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Art. 7 gives the Sultan command of land and sea forces and direction of military movements.

individual-rights-only.rationale: The Rescript and Art. 11 confirm the privileges of religious communities as such, so Ottomanism recognises group rights alongside individual ones.

land-redistribution.rationale: Arts. 21 and 24 guarantee property of lawful title and prohibit confiscation, which cuts against taking estates for redistribution.

land-use-tenure.rationale: Art. 21 guarantees private real property of lawful title.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: The Sultan executes the Seriat and sharia courts hear sharia matters (Arts. 7, 87), but civil affairs go to civil tribunals and the Rescript commissions common codes, and Kemal tied the state to the Seriat; evidence points both ways.

minority-language-support.rationale: The Rescript has codes published in all languages current in the Empire and keeps communal schools, but Art. 18 requires Turkish for office; mixed.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Arts. 3 to 7 of the Constitution place sovereignty in the hereditary House of Osman, with a sacred and irresponsible Sultan holding the major executive powers.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: Ottomanism kept the millet structure, and the Rescript confirms communal privileges, assemblies, schools and their own reform commissions.

national-self-determination.rationale: Ottomanism aimed to hold the empire together under a shared identity against separatist nationalisms, and Art. 1 forbids detaching any part.

night-watchman-state.rationale: The Rescript promises roads, canals and public works and Art. 114 makes primary education compulsory, beyond defence and justice.

office-by-exam.rationale: Art. 19 and Art. 39 fill posts by merit and capacity under regulations, and the Rescript opens schools by examination, though competitive examination is not specified.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Under Arts. 7, 43-44 and 54 no bill becomes law without imperial sanction and the Sultan can dissolve the chamber, though the Assembly legislates and Namik Kemal held that sovereignty comes from the people.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Arts. 10, 23, 25 and 96 require punishment, tribunals and taxes to rest on law and prescribed forms, though the Sultan is irresponsible (Art. 5).

property-fundamental.rationale: Art. 21 guarantees property and forbids dispossession except for public cause after prior payment, and Art. 24 bans confiscation.

racial-franchise.rationale: Arts. 8, 17 and 19 admit all Ottomans to rights and office without distinction of faith, and Art. 68 bars only non-nationals and similar classes.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: The Rescript abolishes every distinction making any class inferior on account of race, and Art. 17 gives all Ottomans equal rights.

religious-nation.rationale: Art. 8 calls all subjects Ottomans whatever faith they profess, and Grigoriadis describes Ottomanism as a civic identity devoid of religious or ethnic underpinnings.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: The Rescript says the laws shall be enforced against any injurious or offensive term, among private individuals or by authorities, about religion, language or race.

right-to-secede.rationale: Art. 1 declares the Empire an indivisible whole from which no portion can be detached under any pretext.

separate-church-state.rationale: Art. 11 makes Islam the state religion, Art. 4 makes the Sultan Supreme Caliph and Art. 87 keeps sharia courts.

separated-powers.rationale: The Constitution sets up separate Senate, Chamber, ministers responsible to the Chamber (Arts. 30-38), and irremovable judges (Art. 81, 86), though the Sultan retains dominant powers.

single-official-language.rationale: Art. 18 makes Turkish the official language for office and Art. 57 the language of debates, while the Rescript orders laws translated into all languages and leaves communal schools; mixed.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: The Sultan is irresponsible and sacred (Art. 5), yet he exercises his rights within the law and Art. 115 forbids suspending the Constitution; mixed.

state-harmful.rationale: The Tanzimat and 1876 programme builds a stronger constitutional state with guarantees and common institutions.

total-state.rationale: Arts. 9, 10, 15 and 22 guarantee personal liberty, free education and inviolable domicile against state direction.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: The Rescript sends mixed suits to common tribunals and orders common codes, yet lets same-faith civil cases go to community councils and Art. 87 keeps sharia courts.

missingStatements.rationale: Both the 1856 Rescript and the 1876 Constitution forbid torture outright and order officials who use it punished.

quotes.text: everything that resembles torture shall be entirely abolished
Torture and inquisition, under any form, are wholly and absolutely forbidden.

missingStatements.text: No one should be compelled to change their religion.
missingStatements.rationale: The Rescript forbids compulsion of religion and the Constitution protects the free exercise of all faiths.

quotes.text: No one shall be compelled to change their religion.
the state will protect the free exercise of faiths professed in the Empire

missingStatements.declined: Read literally, accepted almost everywhere; restrict-conversion covers the contested side.

notes: Draft uses only stated positions of the Tanzimat/1876 programme. Most economic, social, ecological and foreign-policy statements are null because the Rescripts, the Constitution and the scholarship record no position. Themes searched: religion and state, equality and citizenship, parliament and monarchy, courts and rights, property and taxes, provinces and secession, language, education, military, emergency powers.
